Surah Qaf is Meccan, and its verses number forty-five.

﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an.﴾ That is, possessing glory and nobility above all other books; or because it is the speech of the Glorious One; or because whoever knows its meanings and acts upon what is in it will be glorified with God Most High and among the people. The discussion concerning it is like that which was detailed at the beginning of Surah Sad.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 50, verse 2:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, they wonder that a warner has come to them from among themselves﴾. That is: because a warner has come to them of their own kind, not of the kind of an angel, or from among their own flesh and blood. It is a turning away (idrab) from what is indicated by the answer of the omitted oath (jawab al-qasam), as if it were said: "By the glorious Qur'an, We have sent it down to you so that you may warn people by it," as occurs at the beginning of Surat al-A'raf. It is as if it were said: after that, they did not believe in it; rather, they made each of the warner and the thing he warned about an object of denial and wonder, even though both are most fitting to the demands of reason and closest to being received with acceptance. It has also been said: the estimated sense is "By the glorious Qur'an, indeed you are a warner," and then after that it was said that they doubted it, and then it was turned away from. It has also been said: "Rather, they wonder" means that they did not suffice with doubt and rejection, but firmly held the opposite, to the point that they regarded this as one of the strange matters. It has also been said: it is a turning away from what is understood from describing the Qur'an as glorious, as if it were said: the reason for their refusal to believe in the Qur'an is not that it lacks glory, but rather their ignorance.

﴿So the disbelievers said: "This is a strange thing."﴾ This is an explanation of their wonder and a statement that it accompanies the utmost denial, together with further detail about the object of their wonder. "This" is a reference to his, upon him be blessings and peace, being a warner with the Qur'an. Their being referred to by pronoun first serves to indicate that they are identified by what was attributed to them, and their being referred to by explicit noun second serves to record against them disbelief in its implication. Or it is a continuation: their wonder at the sending of a prophet, with "this" pointing to something vague which is explained by the following denying sentence. Placing the explicit noun in the place of the pronoun is either because their characteristic that makes them disbelievers has already preceded, or to indicate that their wonder at resurrection, since it indicates their deeming God, exalted is He, incapable of it, while they witness His power over what is harder than it by the measure of reason, in His wondrous creations, is more heinous than the first and more deeply rooted in being disbelief.

﴿Are we, when we have died and become dust, [to be returned]?﴾ This is a confirmation of the expression of wonder and an emphasis of the denial. The governing element for it is an implied one, which needs no explanation because of how well known it is, and because what follows indicates it. That is: "When we die and become dust, do we return?" as the warner speaks of it and the one warned by him does, along with the complete contrast between us and life at that time. It is also read as "إذا مُتْنا" (idha mutna, "when we died"), in the form of a statement, or with the interrogative particle of denial omitted.

﴿That﴾ refers to the point of dispute.

﴿is a far return﴾ That is, far from the imaginations, the habit, or possibility. It has also been said that "ar-raj'" (the return) here means "al-marju'" (the thing returned to), which is the answer. In that case, the governing element of the adverbial phrase is what the warner announces of the resurrection (al-ba'th).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 50, verse 4:

﴿We have indeed known what the earth diminishes of them.﴾ This is a refutation of their disbelief in resurrection and a removal of it, for whoever's knowledge is all-encompassing and so subtle that it reaches the point of knowing what the earth diminishes of the bodies of the dead, and consumes of their flesh and bones, how could his restoring them to life as they were be deemed improbable? It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Every son of Adam decays, except the coccyx (ʿajb al-dhanab)." And it has been said: "What the earth diminishes of them" means those among them who die and are buried in the earth.

﴿And with Us is a Book preserving (ḥafīẓ).﴾ It is a Book that preserves (ḥāfiẓ) the details of all things, or one that is protected (maḥfūẓ) from alteration. The purpose is either to illustrate His knowledge, may He be exalted, of the universals and particulars of things by the knowledge of one who has a comprehensive book from which he takes everything; or it is an affirmation of His knowledge, may He be exalted, of them by their being fixed in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) with Him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 50, verse 5:

﴿Nay, they denied the truth﴾ — a turning away (idrab) and a transition (intiqal) from describing their earlier heinousness to describing what is even more heinous and more grievous, namely their denial of prophethood, which is established by manifest miracles.

﴿When it came to them﴾ — without any reflection or consideration. It is also read as "lamma jā'ahum" with a kasra on the lam, in which case the lam indicates a specific time (li-l-tawqit), meaning: at the time of his coming to them. It has also been said that "the truth" here refers to the Qur'an, or to the report of the Resurrection.

﴿So they are in a confused matter﴾ — that is, in a state of disorder with no settled footing, from the expression "maraja al-khatam fi usbu'ihi" (the ring moved loosely on his finger), since they say at one time: he is a poet, at another: he is a sorcerer, and at yet another: he is a soothsayer.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 50, verse 6:

﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them﴾: that is, they have been heedless, or blind, so they did not look.

﴿How We built it﴾ in a manner by which they see it at all times.

﴿How We built it﴾: that is, We raised it up without pillars.

﴿And adorned it﴾ with what is in it of stars arranged in a wondrous order.

﴿And it has no cracks﴾: no rifts, because of its smoothness and its freedom from every flaw and defect. Perhaps the delay of this clause is for the sake of observing the rhyme (fawasil, the rhyming endings of verses).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 50, verse 7:

﴿And the earth — We have spread it out﴾, i.e., We have spread it out.

﴿And We have cast into it firmly set mountains﴾, that is, firm mountains (jibal thawabit), from rasa al-shay', when a thing becomes fixed and steady. The expression of them by this description serves to indicate that their casting into the earth is by means of the earth's being made firm by them.

﴿And We have caused to grow therein of every kind of beautiful pair﴾, of every kind (sinf).

﴿Beautiful﴾, i.e., pleasing (hasan).

Tabsira (insight) and dhikra (reminder) are two causes (ʿillatān) for the actions mentioned above in meaning, even though they are in the accusative by the last verb, or by an implied verb in the manner of a resumption (istiʾnaf). That is: We did what We did in order to give insight and to remind.

"For every servant who turns back" (li-kulli ʿabdin munib): that is, one who returns to his Lord, reflecting upon the marvels of His handiwork.

(p-127) And His saying, exalted is He:

"And We sent down from the sky blessed water," i.e., abundant in benefits. This begins the explanation of how the things mentioned, from every beautiful pair, were made to grow. It is coordinated with "We caused to grow" (anbatna), and what lies between them, on the last view, is an interjection (i'tiraḍ) confirming what precedes it and drawing attention to what follows.

"So We caused to grow thereby," i.e., by that water.

"Gardens," many, i.e., trees bearing fruit.

"And grain of the harvest," i.e., the seed of crops that are harvested, such as wheat, barley and the like. The specific mention of the growth of its grain is because it is the primary intended object.

﴿And the date palms﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with "gardens" (jannāt). Mentioning them specifically, although they are included among the gardens, serves to show their excellence over the rest of the trees. Placing "grain" (al-ḥabb) between them emphasizes that each is distinct and set apart from the rest, and it also accords with the rhythm of the verse-endings (fawāṣil, the rhyming ends of verses).

﴿Towering﴾ means tall, or heavy with fruit, from abasqat al-shāt, said of a ewe when she became pregnant. In that case it follows the pattern afʿala, so its form is fāʿil. It has been read as "bāṣiqāt" for the sake of the qāf.

﴿Having spathes stacked one upon another﴾ means arranged one above another. The meaning is either the piling up of the spathes (ṭalʿ) or the abundance of fruit within them. The clause is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) describing "the date palms," in the manner of "towering," by tardīf (synonymous parallelism). Alternatively, it is a ḥāl from the pronoun in "towering," by tadākhul (embedding). Or the ḥāl is the prepositional phrase (al-jārr wa-l-majrūr), and "spathes" is raised by it as its grammatical subject (fāʿil).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 50, verse 11:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿As a provision for the servants﴾ means: so that We may provide for them. It is a reason (ʿillah) for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and We brought forth﴾. The giving of this reason after the first reason given for "We brought forth," namely insight and remembrance, is a reminder that what is obligatory upon the servant is that his benefit from that should be, from the standpoint of remembrance and insight, more important and more primary than his enjoyment of it from the standpoint of provision. It has been said that "provision" (rizqan) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) derived from the meaning of "We brought forth," because bringing forth (al-inbat) is itself a provision.

﴿And We gave life thereby﴾ means: by that water.

﴿a dead land﴾ means: a barren land with no growth in it at all, by Our making it such that it swelled and brought forth all kinds of plants and flowers, so that it began to stir with them after having been lifeless and motionless. The masculine form "dead" (maytan) is used because "land" (baldah) carries the meaning of "town" (balad) and "place."

﴿Thus will be the coming forth﴾: this is a sentence in which the predicate has been placed first, for the purpose of restriction (qasr). "Thus" (dhalika) is a reference to the life derived from the living things, and the sense of distance contained in it is to indicate the elevated rank of that life. That is: like that wondrous life is your life through resurrection from the graves; nothing is contrary to it. In the expression of the bringing forth of plants from the earth by "giving life," and of the life of the dead by "coming forth," there is an exaltation of the matter of growth, a making light of the matter of resurrection, and an establishment of the likeness between the bringing forth of plants and the giving of life to the dead, in order to clarify the method of analogy (qiyas) and bring it closer to people's understanding.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Before them the people of Noah denied﴾ ...etc. It is a resumptive clause (istinaf, a new sentence that begins a fresh topic) brought to establish the truth of resurrection by showing that all the Messengers, peace be upon them, conveyed it, and by showing the punishment of those who denied it.

﴿And the companions of the Rass﴾: It was said that they were among those to whom Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, was sent. And it was said: and it was said, as has passed in detail in Surat al-Furqan.

﴿And Thamud﴾.

﴿And ʿAd and Pharaoh﴾, i.e., he and his people, so that it accords with what precedes it and what follows it. (p-128) ﴿And the brothers of Lut﴾. It has been said: they were among his in-laws, upon him be prayers and peace.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 50, verse 14:

﴿And the companions of al-Ayka (the Thicket)﴾ are among those to whom Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) was sent, other than the people of Madyan.

﴿And the people of Tubba'﴾: their condition has already been explained in Surat al-Dukhan.

﴿Each one denied the messengers﴾ meaning: in what they were sent with of the sacred laws (shara'i'), among which is the resurrection (al-ba'th), upon which they were all unanimous. That is, each of the peoples mentioned denied their messenger, or all of them denied all the messengers in the sense mentioned. The singular pronoun is used in view of the word "each" (kull), or each one of them denied the plurality of messengers, since they agreed on calling to monotheism (tawhid) and warning of the resurrection and the gathering (hashr). Thus, denying one of them is denying all of them. This is clear on the assumption that Tubba' was a messenger; but on the assumption that he was not, which is the more apparent, the meaning of his people's denial of the messengers is their denial of those before them among the messengers who were unanimous on monotheism and the resurrection, and to this Tubba' used to call them.

﴿So My warning became due﴾ meaning: My threat became due and befell them, and it is the word of punishment (kalimat al-'adhab). In this there is consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ) and a threat to them.

**Abu al-Su'ud, *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim*, on Surah 50, verse 15:**

﴿Were We then worn out by the first creation?﴾ This is a resumptive clause (*istinaf*) that affirms the validity of the resurrection (*ba'th*), whose deniers among the destroyed nations have been described. *Al-'ayy bi-al-amr* means inability to do something. It is said: *'ayya bi-al-amr* and *'iyiya bi-hi*, when one is not guided to the way of doing it. The interrogative hamza (*al-hamza*) is for denial (*li-al-inkar*), and the *fa'* (*al-fa'*) is a conjunction (*li-al-'atf*) joining to an implied clause (*muqaddar*) indicated by the word *al-'ayy* in terms of intention (*al-qasd*) and performance (*al-mubashara*). It is as if it were said: "Did We intend the first creation and then become incapable of it, so that one might suppose We are incapable of re-creation?"

﴿Rather, they are in doubt about a new creation.﴾ This is a conjunction (*'atf*) joining to an implied clause indicated by what precedes it. It is as if it were said: "They do not deny Our power over the first creation; rather, they are in confusion and doubt about a new creation that is yet to come, because it contradicts the usual course of things." The indefinite *khalq* (creation) is used to magnify its importance, to signal that it lies beyond the limits of ordinary habits, and to declare that it deserves to be investigated and that knowledge of it deserves attention.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 50, verse 16:

﴿And We have certainly created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him﴾. That is: what his soul speaks to him, as it occurs to the mind. Al-waswasah (whispering) is a faint sound, and from it comes waswas al-huli (the jingling of ornaments). The pronoun refers to "ma" if it is made a relative pronoun (ism mawsul), and the ba' is as in "sawwata bi-kadha" (he made a sound with such-and-such); or it refers to "al-insan" if "ma" is made a verbal noun (masdariyyah), and the ba' is for transitivity.

﴿And We are nearer to him than the jugular vein﴾. That is: We know his state better than one who is nearer to him than the jugular vein. He expressed nearness of knowledge by nearness of essence, as a figure of speech (tajawwuz), because the latter necessitates the former. Habl al-warid (the jugular vein) is a metaphor for extreme closeness. Al-habl means the vein, and its idafah (construction) is explicative (bayaniyyah). The two warid (jugular veins) are two veins flanking the two sides of the neck at its front, connected to the wattin (the aorta/heart-vessel), running from the head down to it. It is said that it was called warid because the spirit comes to it (yariduhu).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 50, verse 17:

﴿When the two receivers receive﴾ is in the accusative case, governed by what is in "closer" (aqrab) of the meaning of the verb. The meaning is: He is subtle, His knowledge reaches what nothing is more hidden than, and He is closer to man than any closer one, at the time when the two guardians (al-hafizan) receive and are taught (yatalaqqanu) what he utters. In this there is a notice that He, exalted is He, is free of need of their safeguarding, because His knowledge encompasses what is hidden from both of them. Rather, that is for the sake of their writing and their guarding of the deeds of the servant and the presenting of their pages on the day when the witnesses (al-ashhad) stand up, and the servant's knowledge of that, along with his knowledge of God's encompassing the details of his conditions, is an informative matter, an increase in kindness toward him in restraining from evil deeds and desiring good deeds. And from him, upon him be prayer and peace: "Indeed the seat of your two angels is upon your two jawbones (thaniyyatayk), your tongue is their pen, your saliva is their ink, and you are running in what does not concern you. Be not shy before God, nor before them." It is also permitted that the receiving of the two angels is an explanation of the nearness, in the sense of: "We are closer to him, observing his deeds," because our guardians and recorders are charged with him.

﴿On the right and on the left, a sitter﴾ means: on the right a sitter, and on the left a sitter, i.e., one who sits, like "jalis" in the sense of "mujalis" (companion), in wording and meaning. So the first is omitted because the second indicates it, as in the saying of one who said:

"He threw me with a matter from which I and my father were innocent, and for the sake of the well he threw me."

It is also said: "fa'il" is applied to the singular and the plural, as in His exalted saying: ﴿And the angels after that are a helper﴾.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 50, verse 18:**

﴿He does not utter any word﴾. That is, he throws out of his mouth whatever is good or bad. It is also read as "مَا يُلْفَظُ" (*ma yulfaẓu*), using the passive form (*al-bina' lil-maf'ul*), where the verb's subject is not stated: "no word is uttered."

﴿except that with him is a watcher, ready﴾. This is an angel who observes his speech and records it. If the speech is good, the recorder is the one "on the right" (*sahib al-yamin*) specifically. Otherwise, he is the one "on the left" (*sahib al-shimal*). The reason for changing the title is clear and needs no explanation. The singular is used, while the two of them are both standing by what proceeds from him, because each of them is a watcher only over what has been entrusted to him, not over what has been entrusted to his companion. This is indicated by the words of God Most High: ﴿ready﴾, that is, prepared and equipped to write what he has been commanded to write, whether good or bad. Whoever does not pay attention to this may imagine that its meaning is: "two watchers, both ready." The singling out of speech for mention is to establish the same ruling for actions by way of the textual indication (*dalalat al-nass*).

Scholars differ about what the two record. It is said that they record everything, even his groaning during illness. It is also said that they record only what contains reward or sin, and this is the more apparent view, as indicated by the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The recorder of good deeds is on a man's right, and the recorder of evil deeds is on his left. The recorder of good deeds is superior to the recorder of evil deeds. When he does a good deed, the angel of the right records it as ten. When he does an evil deed, the companion on the right says to the companion on the left: 'Leave it for seven hours, perhaps he will glorify God or seek forgiveness.'"

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 50, verse 19:

﴿And the agony of death came in truth﴾ After what was mentioned of their disbelief in the Resurrection and the recompense, and that was removed by establishing His power and knowledge, and it was made clear that all their deeds are preserved and recorded against them, He followed that with a statement of what they will inevitably encounter of death and resurrection, and what branches from it of states and terrors. He expressed the occurrence of each of them in the past tense, to announce their certainty and the extreme nearness of their coming. "Sakrat al-mawt" (the agony of death) is its intensity, which takes away the intellect. The "ba'" (bi-) may be for transitivity, as in your saying: "The messenger came with the news," and the meaning is: he brought it, the agony of death, the reality of the matter that the Books of God and His messengers have spoken of, or the reality of the matter and the manifest condition of the dying person's happiness and wretchedness. It was also said: the truth that must necessarily be is death or the recompense, for man was created for it. It may also be for accompaniment (mulabasa), like that in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿grows with the oil﴾, meaning: accompanied by the truth, that is, by the reality of the matter, or by wisdom and a beautiful end. It was also read "sakrat al-haqq bil-mawt" (the agony of the Truth with death), and the meaning is: it is the agony that was prescribed for man according to the requirement of wisdom, and that because of its intensity it necessitates the departure of the soul or follows it. It was said: the "ba'" means "ma'" (with). It was also said: "sakrat al-haqq" is the agony of God, exalted is He, with the idiom that the idafa is for magnification (al-tahwil). (p-130) It was also read "sakarat al-mawt" (the agonies of death).

﴿That﴾ i.e., death.

﴿is what you used to shy away from﴾ i.e., you used to incline away from it and recoil from it, and the address is to mankind, for the aversion from it is by nature common to every individual of them.

﴿And the Horn will be blown.﴾ This is the second blowing.

﴿That﴾ means: the time of that blowing, with an elided genitive (ḥadhf al-muḍāf).

﴿is the Day of the Threat﴾ means: the day of the fulfilment of the threat that was made in this world; that is, the day on which the threat, understood as the promised punishment, takes place. It has also been said that "that" refers to the time understood from "was blown," since the verb, just as it indicates the event, indicates time. The threat is singled out for mention, even though it is also the Day of the Promise, in order to make it terrifying; for this reason the description begins with the state of the disbelievers.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 50, verse 21:

﴿And every soul shall come⦆ of the souls, the righteous and the wicked.

﴿with it a driver and a witness﴾ Although the manner of driving and bearing witness differs according to the differing deeds of the souls, that is: with it are two angels, one of whom drives it to the place of gathering (al-Mahshar), and the other bears witness to its deeds; or a single angel combining both descriptions, as if it were said: with it is an angel who drives it and bears witness against it. It has also been said: the driver is the recorder of the bad deeds, and the witness is the recorder of the good deeds. It has also been said: the driver is the soul itself or its companion (qarin), and the witness is its limbs or its deeds. The position of "ma'aha" (with it) is accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from "kull" (every), since it is annexed to something that has the status of a definite noun, as if it were said: "every soul"; or it is genitive, being a qualifier of "nafs" (soul); or it is nominative, being a qualifier of "kull" (every).

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Certainly you were heedless of this﴾, is reported through an implied saying (qawl), and it is either another attribute (sifah) of "soul" (nafs), or another circumstantial clause (hal) relating to it, or a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) built on a question arising from what precedes it, as if it were said: "What will be done with it?" So it was said: "It is said: Certainly you were heedless of..." etc. The address to everyone is with this, because there is no one except that he has some heedlessness of the Hereafter. It was also said that the address is to the disbeliever. And it was recited (qara'a, a variant recitation) as "kunti" with a kasra on the ta', considering the feminine gender of "soul." The masculine form in the well-known recitation is by interpreting it as "person," as in the verse of Jabalah ibn Hurayth:

O soul, indeed you are delighted with pleasures,
so remember. Will reminding avail you today?

﴿So We removed from you your covering﴾. The covering (ghita') is the veil that conceals the matters of the return (al-ma'ad), namely heedlessness, absorption in sensible things, attachment to them, and confining one's gaze to them.

﴿So your sight today is sharp﴾, piercing, because the obstacle to seeing has been removed. It was also recited with a kasra on the kaf in the three places.

**"And his companion will say"**: that is, the devil assigned to him, pointing to him.

**"This is what is with me, ready"**: that is, this is what is with me and in my possession, ready for Hell, which I have prepared for it through my seducing and misguiding him. It is also said: the angel assigned to him said, pointing to the record of deeds he carries with him: "This is recorded with me, ready," prepared for presentation. If "mā" (what) is taken as descriptive, then "ready" (ʿatīd) is its description; if it is taken as a relative pronoun, then it is either a substitute for it, or a second predicate, or a predicate for an omitted subject.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 50, verse 24:

﴿Cast, both of you, into Hell every stubborn disbeliever﴾ This is an address from Allah, exalted is He, to the driver and the witness, or to the two angels from the guardians of the Fire (p-131). Or it is addressed to one person, by treating the dual of the agent as the dual of the verb and repeating it, like the saying of one who said:

"If you two restrain me, O son of 'Affan, I will be restrained; and if you two leave me, I will protect a honor that is defended."

Or it is on the basis that the alif is a substitute for the nun of emphasis (nun al-ta'kid), treating the connection as if it were a pause (al-waqf). What supports this is that it was read as ﴿alqiyanna﴾ with the light nun (al-nun al-khafifa).

﴿ʿANID﴾: opposing the truth (mu'anid li-l-haqq).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 50, verse 25:

﴿Forbidder of good⁠﴾ (mannā'in lil-khayr), i.e., one who greatly withholds wealth from its obligatory rights. It is said: the meaning of "good" here is Islam, for the verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira when he prevented his brother's sons from it.

﴿Transgressor﴾ (mu'tadin), i.e., a wrongdoer who oversteps the truth.

﴿Doubter﴾ (murib), i.e., one who is in doubt about Allah and about His religion.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (*Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim*) on surah 50, verse 26:

﴿Who set up another god along with Allah﴾ is a *mubtada'* (the subject of a nominal sentence, here taking on the sense of a conditional), whose *khabar* (predicate) is:

﴿Then cast him into the severe punishment﴾. Or it is a *badal* (substitute, in apposition) for "every disbeliever" (*kull kafir*). The statement of the Exalted, ﴿fa-alqiyahu﴾ ("then cast him"), is a *takrir* (repetition) for emphasis. Or it is a *maf'ul* (object) of a hidden verb that is explained by the explicit "fa-alqiyahu."

﴿His companion will say﴾, that is, the devil assigned to him. It is resumed (*istī'nāf*, a new clause that begins without grammatical connection to what precedes it) in the manner of the clauses that occur in the narration of the exchange, because it is an answer to an omitted statement, indicated by His saying ﴿Our Lord, I did not make him transgress﴾. This indicates a prior speech by the disbeliever, in which he offered an excuse, as if he had said: "He made me transgress," and his companion answered by denying it. The attribution of transgression to him is different from the first clause, which must be coordinated (*ʿaṭf*, conjoined) with what precedes it, indicating that the two notions, namely the arrival of every soul together with the two angels and the statement of its companion, occur together.

﴿But he was﴾, namely the disbeliever himself, in essence.

﴿in far error﴾ from the truth. So I helped him in it by seduction and by calling him to it, without compulsion or coercion, as in His saying: ﴿I had no authority over you except that I called you, and you responded to me.﴾

﴿Qāla﴾ (He said) is a resumptive clause (isti'nāf), built upon a question arising from what precedes it, as if it were said: "Then what did Allah the Exalted say?" So it was said: He said, ﴿Do not dispute before Me﴾, i.e., at the place of reckoning and recompense, since there is no benefit in that.

﴿And I had already sent forward to you the warning﴾ concerning transgression in the abode of earning, in My Books and upon the tongues of My messengers. So do not hope to be freed from it by what you are engaged in of pretexts and false excuses. The clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), containing the reason (ta'līl) for the prohibition, in the sense: Do not dispute, when it is established with you that I had sent forward to you the warning, when I said to Iblīs: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you and with whoever follows you of them, all together﴾. So they followed him, turning away from the truth, and there is no basis for disputing at this time. The bāʾ (in bi-l-waʿīd) is either superfluous (zāʾidah) or transitive (muʿaddiyah), on the basis that qaddama means taqaddama. It has also been allowed that qaddamtu be taken as governing the words of His Exalted saying:

﴿Nothing is changed in My word﴾ ...etc. The threat (al-wa'id) may be linked to an omitted element that is a ḥāl (circumstantial qualifier) of either the object (maf'ul) or the subject (fa'il), meaning: "I have indeed presented this word to you accompanied by the threat, joined to it, or I presented it to you as one who threatens you with it. So do not hope that I will change My threat. Pardoning some of the wrongdoers for reasons that call for it is not a change, for the indications of pardon point to the specification of the threat."

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And I am not unjust to the servants﴾ comes to establish the truth in its general aspect (al-wajh al-kullī) and to make clear that the non-change of the word and the realization of what the threat necessitates is not from Him, Exalted is He, without their deserving it. Rather, it is only because of the transgressions that proceeded from them, which necessitate it, as indicated just above. That is: "I am not one who punishes the servants without sin." This is not injustice according to what is established from the principle of the People of the Sunnah (ahl al-Sunnah, the orthodox Sunni community), let alone being excessive injustice. It demonstrates the perfection of His purity, Exalted is He, from that, by depicting it in the form of what is impossible for Him, glory be to Him, to do, namely injustice. The intensive form (ṣīghat al-mubālaghah, the emphatic pattern) is for emphasizing this meaning by presenting the mentioned punishment without sin in the context of extreme injustice. It is said that it is for preserving the plurality of the servants (ʿabīd), from their saying: "So-and-so is unjust (ẓālim) to his slave" and "a great oppressor (ẓallām) to his slaves," on the basis that it is intensive in quantity, not in quality.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 50, verse 30:

﴿On the Day when We say to Hell, "Are you filled?" and it says, "Are there any more?"﴾ This is a question and an answer, presented in the manner of depiction and imagery (tamthil wa-takhyil) in order to magnify its terror. The meaning is: despite its vastness and the distance of its horizons, there are cast into it, from the jinn and mankind, group after group, until it is filled. Or, [the meaning is that] by its immensity, one who enters it does so while there is still an empty place within it. Or, [the meaning is that] out of its rage against the disobedient, it seeks their increase. "Yaqulu" (he says) has also been read with the letter ya' (yaqulu), and "al-mazid" (the more) is either a verbal noun like "al-mahid" and "al-majid," or a passive participle (maf'ul) like "al-mabi'" (the sold). "Yawma" (on the Day) is either governed by "udhkur" (remember) or "andhir" (warn), or is an adverbial of time governed by "nufikha" (is blown), in which case "dhalika" (that) would be a reference back to it without need of a supplied governing noun, or it is governed by a delayed supplied predicate, meaning: on that Day there will be among the states and terrors what speech falls short of describing.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 50, verse 31:

﴿And Paradise will be brought near to the God-conscious (al-muttaqin)﴾ This begins the explanation of the state of the believers after the Trumpet blast and the coming of souls to the place of reckoning. The secret of placing the state of the disbelievers before it has already been discussed. It is coordinated (ʿatf) with "was blown" (nufikha), meaning: it is brought near for the God-conscious, who have guarded themselves against disbelief and sins, in such a way that they see it from the place of standing and become aware of the various kinds of its beauties; thus they rejoice that they are being gathered toward it and will be triumphant in it. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿not far away﴾ is an emphasis on the bringing near (izlaf), meaning: a place not far away, such that they see it; or it is a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: while it is not far away, i.e., a thing not far away. It is also permissible that the masculine form is used because it is on the pattern of a verbal noun (masdar), which applies equally to the masculine and the feminine in description, or because Paradise is interpreted as a garden (bustan).

This is the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 50, verse 32:

﴿This is what you were promised﴾ is a reference to Paradise. The use of the demonstrative (hadha, "this") is because the one pointed to is the named thing itself, without any word coming to mind that signifies it, let alone its masculine or feminine form, for these two are features of the Arabic word, as has been noted in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when he saw the sun rising, he said: "This is my Lord"﴾, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when the believers saw the confederates, they said: "This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us"﴾. It is also permissible that this (the masculine demonstrative) is used to refer to the news (khabar). It has been said: it is a reference to the reward (thawab). It has been said: it refers to the verbal noun (masdar) of "uzlifat" (was brought near). It has been read as "yū'adūn" (you are promised, in the plural and the passive). The clause is either a parenthetical insertion (i'tirad) between the substitute (badal) and the element substituted for (mubdal minhu), or it is implicitly governed by a verb of saying, and it is in the accusative of circumstance (hal) relating to "al-muttaqin" (the God-fearing) or to "al-jannah" (the Garden), with the governing element being "uzlifat", meaning: "said to them" or "said concerning it": this is what you were promised.

﴿For every penitent (awwab)﴾: that is, one who returns (rajja') to Allah, exalted is He. It is a substitute (badal) for "al-muttaqin" with the preposition repeated.

﴿who keeps watch (hafiz)﴾: one who guards his repentance from deficiency. It has been said: he is the one who keeps watch over his sins until he turns back from them and seeks forgiveness for them. It has been said: he is the one who guards the commands of Allah, exalted is He. It has been said: he guards what Allah, exalted is He, has entrusted to him of its rights.

(p-133) ﴿Whoever feared the Most Merciful unseen and came with a penitent heart﴾ is either a substitute of a substitute, or a substitute of the described noun "awwab" (one who often turns back in repentance). It cannot be in its (the "awwab" word's) position, because whoever is not described by it, and is not described except by "alladhi" (the one who), or is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is...

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 50, verse 34:

﴿Enter it﴾ is in the sense of "It will be said to them: Enter it," and the plural is in view of the meaning of "man" (man, "whoever"). His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in fear unseen﴾ (bil-ghayb) is connected to an omitted element, and is a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the subject of "feared" (khashiya), or from its object, or a qualifier of its verbal noun (masdar), meaning: a fear accompanied by the unseen, since he feared His punishment while it was hidden from the eyes, and no one sees it. The mention of the title "the Most Merciful" (al-Rahmaniyya) is to indicate that they, despite their fear of His punishment, hope for His mercy; or that their knowledge of the vastness of His mercy, exalted is He, restrains them from fearing Him, exalted is He, and that they act in accordance with the requirement of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful. And that My punishment is the painful punishment.﴾ And the describing of the heart as penitent (munib) is because the consideration is its return to God, exalted is He.

﴿In peace﴾ (bi-salam) is connected to an omitted element, and is a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the subject of "Enter it", meaning: accompanied by safety from punishment and the cessation of blessings' loss; or, in peace from the side of God, exalted is He, and His angels.

﴿That﴾ is a reference to the extended period of time in which some of the matters mentioned occurred.

﴿The Day of Eternity﴾ (yawm al-khulud), since it has no end, ever.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 50, verse 35:

﴿Theirs shall be whatever they wish﴾ from the various kinds of desires, whatever it may be.

﴿Therein﴾ is connected to "they wish" (yashā'ūna). It was also said: it is connected to an omitted element, which is a circumstantial clause (hal) either from the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) or from its omitted resumptive pronoun within its relative clause.

﴿And with Us is an increase﴾ is what does not occur to their minds and is not included within their desires, of the sublime honours that no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and that has not occurred to the heart of any human being. It was also said: clouds will pass over the people of Paradise, raining down upon them the Houris, and they will say: "We are the increase (al-mazid) of which God Most High spoke: ﴿And with Us is an increase﴾."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 50, verse 36:

﴿And how many generations We destroyed before them﴾, that is: before your people (qawmika).

﴿Generations stronger than them in might﴾, that is: in strength, like 'Ad and their likes.

﴿So they roamed through the lands﴾, that is: they pierced through them (kharaqu fiha), subdued them, and gained control over their regions; or they traversed every passage in the sides of the earth fleeing from death. The original meaning of tanqib (roaming/searching) and naqb (a hole or passage) is: to dig out information about a matter, to search, and to seek. The fa' (so) indicates that the severity of their might enabled them to roam. It has been said: it is an 'atfah (coordinating conjunction) in meaning, as if it were said: their might was severe, so they roamed... etc. It was also read with the lighter form (fa-naqqaw, with the doubled letter not stressed, read as "faqqabu").

﴿Was there any escape?﴾, that is: was there for them any deliverer from the command of God Most High? The clause is either on the assumption of an implied saying, which is a circumstantial (hal) clause from the waw of "naqqabu", meaning: so they roamed through the lands saying, "Is there any escape?"; or by treating the roaming, because of what it contains of the meaning of tracing and searching, as if it were a saying; or it is an independent statement, coming to deny that they had any escape. It has been said: the pronoun in "naqqabu" refers to the people of Makkah, meaning: they traveled in their journeys and travels in the lands of the generations, so did they see any escape for them, so that they might hope for the like for themselves? This is supported by the reading in the imperative form, and it was read "fa-naqqibu" with a kasra on the qaf, from the naqab, which is when the camel's hoof is worn through, meaning: they journeyed so much that their feet or their camels' hooves were worn through.

(p-134) ﴿Indeed, in that﴾ — i.e., in what has been mentioned of their story. It has also been said: in what has been mentioned in the surah.

﴿is surely a reminder﴾ — a admonition and an exhortation.

﴿for whoever has a heart﴾ — i.e., a sound heart by which he perceives the true reality of the matters he witnesses and reflects upon them as he should. For whoever has this will know that the root of their ruin is disbelief, and so he refrains from it merely by seeing the traces, without any need for admonition.

﴿or gives ear﴾ — i.e., to what is recited to him of the revelation that speaks of what befell them. For whoever does this comes to know the clear truth of the matter and is restrained from what leads to disbelief. Thus the word "or" (aw) indicates that the two are alternatives, not that both must be combined, for merely giving ear is of no benefit without a sound heart, as His saying, Exalted is He, hints: ﴿and he is a witness﴾ — i.e., present with his understanding, for one whose mind is not present is as if absent. And the stripping of the heart of the attributes mentioned is to make clear that whoever has his heart emptied of them is like one who has no heart at all.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 50, verse 38:

﴿And We certainly created the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾ of the kinds of created things.

﴿in six days﴾ and ﴿We did not suffer any fatigue﴾ from that, although it is something that powers and capacity cannot bear.

﴿from fatigue﴾: from any weariness at all, nor any exhaustion in general. This is a refutation of the ignorant Jews in their claim that God, exalted is He, began the creation of the world on Sunday, finished it on Friday, rested on Saturday, and reclined upon the Throne, glorified is He and exalted far above what they say, exalted to a great degree.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 50, verse 39:

﴿So be patient over what they say.﴾ That is: over the falsehoods the polytheists say concerning the Resurrection, which are founded on denial and disbelief in its possibility. For He who did these deeds without weariness is able to resurrect them and to take vengeance upon them. Or it refers to what the Jews say of the statements of disbelief and anthropomorphism (tashbih).

﴿And glorify your Lord with His praise﴾ That is: declare your Lord exalted (nazzih) above incapacity regarding what is possible, and above the occurrence of falsehood in His reports, among which is the report of the occurrence of the Resurrection, and above describing Him with attributes that necessitate anthropomorphism, praising Him for what He has bestowed upon you, such as reaching the truth and other things.

﴿Before the rising of the sun and before its setting﴾ These are the times of Fajr (dawn prayer) and 'Asr (afternoon prayer), and their virtue is well known.

And from the night, glorify Him too, (﴿وَمِنَ اللَّيْلِ فَسَبِّحْهُ﴾) and glorify Him during part of the night.

﴿وَأدْبارَ السُّجُودِ﴾ and at the adbar (ends) of the prostrations, i.e., the following of the prayers. It is the plural of dubur, and it has been read with a kasra (adbira) from "adbarat al-salah," meaning when the prayer has ended and been completed. Its meaning is: the time of the ending of the prostration. It has also been said that the intended glorification is the prayers. Thus, what is meant by "before the rising" is the Fajr prayer, by "before the setting" the Dhuhr and 'Asr prayers, and by "part of the night" the two 'Isha' prayers and the tahajjud (night prayer). And what is prayed "after the prostrations" (adbar al-sujud) refers to the supererogatory prayers after the obligatory ones.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 50, verse 41:**

﴿And listen﴾ means: to what is revealed to you about the conditions of the Resurrection. In this there is a magnification and a dreadful portrayal of what is being reported.

﴿On the day the Caller calls﴾ means: Israfil or Jibril, peace be upon them both, who will say: "O decayed bones, O torn flesh, and O scattered hair, indeed God commands you to gather together for the decisive judgment." It is also said: Israfil blows (the trumpet) and Jibril calls for the gathering.

﴿from a near place﴾ means: in such a way that his call reaches everyone equally (p-135). It is also said: from the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It is said: from beneath their feet. It is said: from the roots of their hair, so that it is heard from every single hair. Perhaps that in the restoration is like "Be" at the beginning.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 50, verse 42:

﴿The Day they hear the Cry in truth﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿the Day the Caller calls﴾ ... and so on. The Cry is the second blast (al-nafkha al-thaniya).

﴿in truth﴾ is connected to "the Cry." The governing element (al-'amil) of the adverbial phrase of time is what is indicated by the words of the Exalted: ﴿That is the Day of Coming Forth﴾. That is: the Day they hear the Cry accompanied by the truth, which is the Resurrection (al-ba'th), when they come forth from the graves.

**Verse 43:** ﴿Indeed, it is We who give life and cause death﴾ in this world, with no one sharing with Us in that.

﴿And to Us is the final return﴾ for recompense in the Hereafter, not to other than Us, neither independently nor jointly.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 50, verse 44:

﴿On the Day the earth splits asunder from them﴾ with the deletion of one of the two tâʾs in "tatashaqqaqu" (the verb "tatashaqqaqu," "splits," with one of its two tâʾs omitted). It is also read with the shîn doubled (tashshaqqaqu), and "tushaqqaqu" in the passive form from the taf'îl pattern, and "tanshaqqu."

﴿sirâʿan﴾ (swiftly): hastening.

﴿That is a gathering﴾: resurrection (baʿth), assembling (jamʿ), and driving (sawq).

﴿upon Us is easy﴾: i.e., easy (hayyin). The fronting of the prepositional phrase "ʿalaynâ" (upon Us) is to restrict ease to Him, exalted is He.

﴿We know best what they say﴾, of denial of the resurrection, denial of the verses that clearly speak of it, and other things in which there is no good.

﴿And you are not over them a tyrant﴾, one who compels them to faith or does to them whatever he wishes. Rather, you are only a reminder.

﴿So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning﴾. As for those other than them, We shall inflict upon them the various kinds of punishment and forms of torment that their words call for and their deeds demand. From the Prophet, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him, [it is reported]: "Whoever recites Surat Qaf, Allah will make easy for him the pangs of death and its agonies."
